title: The seven mansions
hook: Teresa's castle has seven dwelling places, and the King lives in the center
carry: the king is in the center

segments.voice: Yesterday, four ways to water a garden: buckets, a wheel, a stream, and rain. Your line was sometimes buckets, sometimes rain. Which one was your day? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

Later, Teresa is asked to write again, this time for her sisters. She says she didn't know how to begin. Then a new picture came to her: the soul as a castle, made of a single diamond or very clear crystal, with many rooms. Some rooms above, some below, some to the sides. And in the very center, the main room, where the most secret things pass between God and the soul. The King lives there. Plenty of souls, she says, stay out in the courtyard, around the outer wall, with no idea what's inside their own house. The book she wrote is called The Interior Castle, and she groups its rooms into seven dwelling places. Today: the seven mansions.
screen: `MANY ROOMS, AND ONE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Teresa took the word from Jesus. In John's Gospel he says, "In my Father's house are many mansions." In the King James English, mansion means a dwelling place, a room to stay in, not a big house on a hill. Teresa's Spanish word is moradas, dwellings. So the seven mansions aren't seven buildings. They're seven depths of one soul, the way rooms go further into a house. How do you get in? Her answer is simple: the door of this castle is prayer and reflection. Not cleverness, not a special technique. Just turning toward God, honestly, and paying attention. The outer rooms are crowded. She says snakes and vermin from outside creep in with you there: distractions, worries, the business of the day. That's not a reason to stay out. It's just what the first rooms are like. Further in, it gets quieter. The light from the center reaches further. Prayer becomes less something you do and more something that happens to you, like yesterday's rain. And then the startling part. In Teresa's picture, the King isn't somewhere far away, waiting at the end of the road. He's in the center of the soul, already. The castle is beautiful because he's in it, Teresa says, and nothing we do can take that beauty away, though sin can cover it, like a black cloth thrown over a crystal in the sun. The light is still shining underneath. For Teresa, the journey inward isn't a hunt for a God who's missing. It's coming home to the room where, she says, he has been the whole time.
screen: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE ARE MANY MANSIONS.`
`THE KING IS ALREADY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go one room further in. Sit and let your breath slow. Notice where you are right now, in Teresa's picture. Out in the courtyard, with the noise? In one of the first rooms, where the worries crawl in too? Don't fight that. Just take one step further: one more breath of attention, one layer quieter. If you pray, you can turn toward the King at the center, without needing to reach him. If you don't, just notice that there's an inside, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
The seven mansions. Teresa's dwelling places of the soul, one inside another, opening toward the center, where the King lives.
Your line: the king is in the center. Today, when the courtyard gets loud, take one step inward before you answer it. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Carmelites and others who pray in Teresa's way read The Interior Castle slowly, often with a spiritual director, and speak of prayer as a journey inward toward God dwelling at the center of the soul.
